clue.text: Speaker in court upset judge

parts.note: to be in court with someone, paying court, is to woo them

indicators.note: upset means knocked over, so the letters are turned back to front

parts.note: a ref, short for referee, judges a match

explanation.surface: A courtroom scene where someone speaks out and the judge is put out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Upset' turns REF round to FER. 'In court' suggests a law court, but court here means wooing. A woofer is the loudspeaker unit for bass sounds.
explanation.definitionFit: A woofer is the large loudspeaker driver in a sound system that reproduces low bass notes.

clue.text: Humpty Dumpty figure, typically round and hollow

parts.note: the letter O is round
void = empty, hollow

explanation.surface: A description of the nursery-rhyme egg: round and empty inside.
explanation.walkthrough: Humpty Dumpty is traditionally drawn as an egg, and 'typically' flags that his shape is one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means egg-shaped, from Latin ovum, and nursery-rhyme illustrations always draw Humpty as an egg.

clue.text: Briefed about retaining least depleted feature of sewage works

indicators.note: retaining means holding inside, so the rearranged letters keep the next pair within them
about here means in a state of disorder, so the letters of briefed are rearranged
depleted means emptied, so least loses its inner letters and leaves only its first and last

parts.note: with its middle removed, least gives L and T

explanation.surface: Someone instructed about the least worn-out part of a sewage plant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Depleted' empties least to LT, which the jumble of Briefed, made by 'about', holds as 'retaining' says. A filter bed is a tank of gravel or sand that cleans sewage.
explanation.definitionFit: A filter bed is a layer of sand or gravel through which sewage is passed for cleaning, a standard part of a treatment plant.

clue.text: Verses of short song, cutting about Starmer primarily

indicators.note: cutting means slicing into, so the shortened song sits between the other letters

parts.note: re is Latin for about, as in letter headings

indicators.note: primarily means first of all, so the opening letter

parts.note: the first letter of Starmer, the British Prime Minister

indicators.note: short means the word is cut off before its final letter

parts.note: a hymn is a religious song

explanation.surface: A political lyric: a short song mocking Keir Starmer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Short' trims HYMN to HYM, which cuts into RE plus S, the first of Starmer.
explanation.definitionFit: Rhymes are short pieces of verse, as in nursery rhymes, so the plural word stands for verses.

clue.text: Hiss and abuse boxing team across Belgium

indicators.note: to box something in is to enclose it

parts.note: to slate = to criticise harshly; its S and LATE wrap round the middle

indicators.note: lying across something straddles it

parts.note: a football or cricket team is 11, written here as two ones
B is Belgium's international vehicle code

explanation.surface: Someone hisses and hurls insults at a sports team playing in Belgium.
explanation.walkthrough: Crossword teams are usually XI; here the number 11 is written with two ones, which is the step most solvers miss.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym, from Latin sibilare: the verb means producing a sustained s-sound, as snakes and whisperers do.

clue.text: Nothing whatsoever in a few nasty names roughly embodying Democrat?

indicators.note: done roughly means not done precisely, so the letters come out of order
to embody something is to take it into your body

parts.note: anagram fodder, 14 letters
D = Democrat

explanation.surface: A US Democrat is being called a few rude names.
explanation.walkthrough: The phrase, often shortened to 'sweet FA', is British slang; it began as Navy slang for tinned meat.
explanation.definitionFit: British idiom: the phrase, a polite stand-in for a ruder expression, means absolutely nothing, as in 'we got sweet FA for it'.

clue.text: Time Bill lifted hearts in place where Robin drinks?

parts.note: bird is British slang for a prison sentence, time served

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifted means raised up, so the word reads from the bottom upward

parts.note: a tab is a bill, as in running up a tab
H is the card abbreviation for hearts

explanation.surface: A tale of a crook named Bill doing time, with Robin Hood in the background.
explanation.walkthrough: BIRD for time is prison slang. 'Lifted' turns TAB upward to BAT. Robin looks like a name, but it is the garden bird, and the question mark flags the example.
explanation.definitionFit: A birdbath is a shallow basin in a garden where small birds such as robins drink and wash.

clue.text: Pressure group left flyer, hard to ignore

parts.note: L = left
HOBBY, a small falcon, without H for hard

explanation.surface: A campaign group has left a leaflet that is hard to ignore.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flyer' reads as a leaflet in the campaigning surface, but here it is the hobby, a small falcon.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: organised interests that try to sway politicians were named after the parliamentary hall where they buttonholed members.

clue.text: Chance to work with elite, no frills specialist

indicators.note: letters set to work are put through their paces
frills are trimmings at the edge, so ELITE loses its first and last letters

parts.note: anagram fodder, taken as printed
ELITE without its first and last E

explanation.surface: A job offer to work with top people, in a no-frills setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chance' is used as printed rather than swapped for a synonym, and 'no frills' reads as budget rather than as trimming.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym, both adjectives: jargon or knowledge belonging to one expert field is described with either word.

clue.text: Insect Australian sheep tolerate

parts.note: woolly is Australian slang for a sheep
to bear = to tolerate

explanation.surface: An Australian sheep puts up with an insect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Australian' makes you look for a country or an abbreviation, but it names the slang: in Australia a sheep can be called a woolly.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: the hairy caterpillar of the tiger moth goes by this name, and a larva still counts as an insect.

clue.text: Rugby player struck ultimately by taxi travelling west

indicators.note: an across entry reads eastward, so heading west means reading right to left
ultimately means in the end, so only the final letter of struck is used

parts.note: last letter of struck
a cab is a taxi; K is set next to it, then the whole K CAB turns round

explanation.surface: A rugby player is hit by a taxi heading west.
explanation.walkthrough: The accident scene makes 'struck by taxi' one idea, but 'by' only puts K beside CAB before the pair is reversed.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: in rugby the players stationed behind the scrum, such as wingers and full-backs, are collectively called by this name.

clue.text: Supporter of approach where very little is changed for that woman

indicators.note: where points into the approach word, marking it as the place the change happens
something changed for another is swapped out

parts.note: an advent is an arrival, an approach
V = very, and it is only one letter
her = that woman

explanation.surface: A backer of a policy under which a tiny amount is swapped for a woman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Very little' describes a single letter: V, the abbreviation for very, is what gets replaced.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: someone who sticks to a cause or leader, from Latin adhaerere, to cling, is a follower or backer.

clue.text: US singer missing extremely creative day in past

indicators.note: missing means lacking, so the following letters are taken away

parts.note: Beyonce is the American singer

indicators.note: extremely means at the extremes, so only the first and last letters

parts.note: the outer letters of creative are C and E

explanation.surface: An American pop star, no longer so creative, long past her best day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Extremely' gives CE from creative, which 'missing' takes from BEYONCE, leaving BEYON before D.
explanation.definitionFit: Beyond and past both mean further than, as in 'past the church' or 'beyond the church'.

clue.text: Youngster defending Student Union

indicators.note: a defender surrounds what it protects

parts.note: a cub is a young animal, or a young scout; it opens to take L
L = learner, a student

explanation.surface: A young person stands up for the students' union.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Student Union' looks like one institution; it splits, with Student giving L and Union the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: an association of members joined by a shared interest, such as a golf or book society.

clue.text: Rock ace not "semi-literate", revolutionary claims

indicators.note: a revolution turns something right round, so the hidden letters read upward
to claim something is to take hold of it, so the phrase holds the answer inside

parts.note: acE NOT SEMI-Literate, to be read backwards

explanation.surface: A rock-star ace insists he is not semi-literate, and a revolutionary makes claims.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rock ace' reads as a guitar hero, and the quotation marks make 'semi-literate' look like the thing to decode, but the letters simply run backwards through the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a sedimentary stone formed mainly of calcium carbonate, used for building and cement.

clue.text: Object found in transport café, traditionally on the counter

indicators.note: something found in a place is inside it, so the answer lies within the phrase
counter means running against, so the letters are read against the usual direction

parts.note: transporT CAFÉ, TRAditionally, to be read backwards

explanation.surface: Something left on the counter of a roadside café, as is the custom.
explanation.walkthrough: The café scene makes 'counter' the thing you order at; here it means going against the reading direction. A transport café is a cheap British roadside diner for lorry drivers.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a man-made item, especially one of historical interest dug up by archaeologists, is called this.

clue.text: Spooner's curious electrical device that's used in the kitchen

definitions.note: a descriptive phrase: 'something that's used in the kitchen'

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner was famous for swapping the opening sounds of words

parts.note: prying = nosy, curious
an electric fan
swap the P and F sounds

explanation.surface: An odd electric gadget found in someone's kitchen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Electrical device that's used in the kitchen' looks like the definition of a blender; the device is only the fan, and the kitchen item is not electric at all.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by description: a shallow long-handled pan for cooking eggs and bacon on the hob is a kitchen staple.

clue.text: Bull, perhaps, from present US president

parts.note: present = here, as in a register
Gerald Ford, 38th US president

explanation.surface: A gift of a bull from the current American president.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present US president' reads as whoever is in office now; present is split off as HERE, and the president is Ford.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a red-and-white English breed of beef cattle, so a bull may belong to it; 'perhaps' marks the example.

clue.text: A little dog is with men on manoeuvres

indicators.note: troops on manoeuvres move about in the field, so the letters shift position

parts.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder, joined by 'with'

explanation.surface: A small dog accompanies soldiers on an army exercise.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A little dog' reads as a puppy; 'A little' is the definition and 'dog' is fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym: a tiny amount, as in 'just a smidgen of milk'; this spelling is a less common variant.

clue.text: Daughter departs put off about Connecticut college

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the remaining letters are read backwards
departs means leaves, so that letter goes from the word

parts.note: to delay something is to put it off

explanation.surface: A daughter leaving for an American college after putting it off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Departs' takes D from DELAY, leaving ELAY, which 'about' turns round.
explanation.definitionFit: Yale is the Ivy League university in New Haven, Connecticut.

clue.text: Root striking ball matching Pope's last run

indicators.note: striking means striking out, so the letter is deleted

parts.note: going means matching, as when colours go together
O looks like a ball

indicators.note: the possessive last means the final letter belonging to the Pope

parts.note: Pope ends in E
R is the cricket abbreviation for run

explanation.surface: A cricket picture: hitting a ball for a run, alongside the Pope.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Striking' removes O from GOING, giving GING; 'last' of Pope gives E. Root is the definition, as ginger is a rhizome used in cooking.
explanation.definitionFit: Ginger is the spicy underground stem of a tropical plant, sold and cooked as a root.

clue.text: Mind whisper principal murmured

indicators.note: a murmur is spoken softly, so only the sound of the words counts

parts.note: a sigh is a whisper of breath; key = principal, as in key figure

explanation.surface: An instruction to whisper something to the head teacher.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Principal' reads as a school head, but it is the adjective: key.
explanation.definitionFit: Plain synonym, from Greek for breath or soul: psychologists use it for the whole human mental self.

clue.text: Cycle bent round tree

parts.note: bent into a round shape = arced; AR then moves to the end

explanation.surface: A bicycle, its frame bent, wrapped round a tree after a crash.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cycle' looks like a bike in the crash scene; it tells you to rotate the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Definition by example: a tall coniferous evergreen of Lebanon and the Himalayas, prized for fragrant timber.

clue.text: Diamond, say, extra pay at intervals secures, reversing transfer

indicators.note: things spaced at intervals have gaps between them, so every other letter is taken
to secure something is to hold it fast
reversing goes backwards, so the whole assembled string is turned round

parts.note: ExTrA pAy, every other letter; NEIL goes before the final A
Neil Diamond, the American singer

explanation.surface: An odd payroll instruction: a diamond or a bonus is secured, then the transfer is reversed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Diamond, say' looks like a gem, a pitch or a card; it is Neil Diamond, whose name reads backwards in the middle of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Legal sense: handing ownership of property to someone else is to alienate it, which is why rights can be inalienable.

clue.text: Military volunteers once getting letter from Crete?

definitions.meaning: split 3-1-1: the article plus the initials of Britain's former part-time reserve army
a character of the Greek alphabet, as used on the island

explanation.surface: Old army volunteers receive a letter posted from Crete.
explanation.walkthrough: Split three-one-one, the answer is the Territorial Army, Britain's volunteer reserve until it became the Army Reserve in 2014. The question mark admits the letter is from the Greek alphabet, not the post.
explanation.definitionFit: Two senses: the eighth Greek alphabet character, used on Crete, and the article plus the abbreviation of Britain's former part-time army.

clue.text: Become very angry leaving automatic essentially in "Drive"

indicators.note: leaving means departing, so the letter is taken out

parts.note: to go mad is to become very angry

indicators.note: essentially means at its heart, so the middle letter

parts.note: the central letter of automatic is M

explanation.surface: A driver enraged at an automatic gearbox.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Essentially' gives M, the centre of automatic, and 'leaving' takes it from GO MAD. Drive is a verb here, as in driving cattle.
explanation.definitionFit: To goad is to urge or prod someone on, which matches drive in the sense of pushing forward.

clue.text: Limits wearing old DJ and possibly tangerine jacket

parts.note: O = old
the range of something is its limits
John Peel, the long-serving BBC radio DJ

explanation.surface: An old DJ's taste stretches as far as a tangerine-coloured jacket.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tangerine jacket' reads as a loud piece of clothing; the jacket is the fruit's skin, and 'possibly' marks a tangerine as one kind of orange.
explanation.definitionFit: Playful description: the skin wrapped round a citrus fruit is its jacket, and a tangerine is one variety of that fruit.

clue.text: Wanting golf game, ambassador succeeded to tour islands

indicators.note: to tour means going all round, so the pair wraps round the other part

parts.note: HE is His Excellency, the style of an ambassador
S is the abbreviation for succeeded in family trees

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so the letter is removed

parts.note: bridge is a card game
G is golf in the NATO phonetic alphabet

explanation.surface: An envoy, having given up golf, takes a tour of the islands.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wanting' takes G from BRIDGE to give BRIDE, which HE plus S goes round, as 'to tour' says. The Hebrides are islands off western Scotland.
explanation.definitionFit: The Hebrides are the chain of islands off the west coast of Scotland, Inner and Outer.

clue.text: Catwalk model wary around Quant occasionally

indicators.note: around means surrounding, so the reshaped letters wrap round the others
to model is to shape, so the letters of wary are reshaped
occasionally means now and then, so alternate letters

parts.note: taking every other letter of Quant gives U and N

explanation.surface: A fashion model nervous on the catwalk around designer Mary Quant.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Occasionally' takes UN from Quant, set inside RWAY, the reshaping of wary signalled by 'model'. Mary Quant was the 1960s British fashion designer of the miniskirt.
explanation.definitionFit: A runway is the long raised platform on which models parade at a fashion show.
